01KXQQZHJH6B0BY3KX1VVMA0TJ.title: Ragionamento di Luca Contile sopra la proprietà delle imprese con le particolari de gli Academici Affidati et con le interpretationi et croniche

evidence: Worthington, bookplate; Kerr & Richardson, Glasgow, bookseller’s label at end; T

Provenance: W.D. Worthington, bookplate; Kerr & Richardson, Glasgow, bookseller’s label at end; T. Kimball Brooker (Bibliotheca Brookeriana, VIII, lot 95). Original edition of this lavishly printed emblem book divided into two parts. The first part (ll. 1-43), after briefly discussing medals and hieroglyphics, deals with devices from a theoretical point of view by raising specific questions. The author, who demonstrates to be well aware of his predecessors’ writings on the subject (citing, among others, Paradin, Giovio, Domenichi, Ruscelli, Ammirato, and Arnigio), distinguishes between crests, coat-of-arms, hieroglyphics, emblems, and devices, seeking to define how the latter differ from the former: the device, which in his opinion is “componimento di figura e di motto rappresentando vertuoso e magnanimo disegno” (‘a composition of figure and motto representing a virtuous and magnanimous design’), is only suitable for virtuous characters and not for “li tinti d’infamia et i professori dell’arti meccaniche, eccettuati gl’ingegneri che stanno a’ servigi de’ principi, i pittori eccellenti e gli statuarii famosi” (‘those tainted with infamy and those practicing mechanical arts, except for engineers who are in the service of princes, excellent painters, and famous sculptors’). The second part, on the other hand, is a veritable tribute to the members of the Accademia degli Affidati, whose devices are extensively commented on and enriched with numerous biographical details. The devices include that of Contile himself (l. 83), in which he provides valuable information about his life, and that of San Carlo Borromeo (l. 86).Towards the end of April 1574, the printing of Contile’s Ragionamento was finally completed, and on August 23, he sent a copy of the newly printed book to the Duke of Parma, informing him that the edition had been ready for four months and, complaining about the quality of the printing, he was hoping for a

Sansovino Francesco.name: Sansovino Francesco
biographies: Francesco Tatti, generally known as Francesco Sansovino, was born in Rome in 1521 and died in Venice on 28 September 1583. He was teh son of the Florentine sculptor and architect Jacopo Tatti, called Sansovino. Baptised in the Roman church of Sant’Eustachio, he had as godfather Giovanni Maria del Monte, the future Pope Julius III. The Sack of Rome in 1527 compelled the family to leave the city, passing through Florence before settling in Venice, where Jacopo entered the service of the Procurators of Saint Mark. Francesco consequently grew up close to the political, artistic, and ceremonial centre of the Republic, although he continued to present himself as Florentine by descent and linguistic allegiance and Venetian by adoption. He also published under the names Anselmo Guisconi and Giovanni Tatti. His education combined humanist letters with the legal studies preferred by his father. Stefano Piazzone da Asola and Giovita Ravizza instructed him in Latin grammar and rhetoric, while Antonio Francini da Montevarchi introduced him to Greek. In 1536 he went to Padua to study law, but also attended the lectures of the classicist Lazzaro Bonamico. His admission to the Accademia degli Infiammati in 1540 placed him within a particularly consequential forum for discussion of rhetoric, philosophy, ethics, and the extension of learned discourse into the vernacular. Among the figures associated with this environment were Sperone Speroni, Alessandro Piccolomini, Benedetto Varchi, Bernardino Tomitano, Marco Mantova Benavides, and Mariano Sozzini. Sansovino became an affiliate of the Accademia Fiorentina in January 1542 and subsequently moved to Bologna, where in 1543 he received a doctorate in civil law. His unpublished Dialogo della pratica della ragione, composed during this formative period, stages an encounter between Bartolus of Sassoferrato and Machiavelli and reveals an early attempt to reconcile juristic tradition with the political language of the Renaissance. Letters exchanged with Pietro Aretino document both Sansovino’s youthful literary ambitions and his gradual resistance to a conventional legal career. By the early 1540s he was already writing poetry, compiling texts, and participating in the editorial culture of Venice. He collaborated with Lodovico Dolce on an edition of Aretino’s verse and published the Lettere sopra le diece giornate del Decamerone in 1542, followed by a short Rhetorica in 1543. His Venetian acquaintances included Dolce, Gaspara Stampa, Giuseppe Betussi, Lodovico Domenichi, Francesca Baffo, and other writers whose careers were closely connected with the presses. He worked as a corrector and editorial assistant, notably in the orbit of the Giolito press, acquiring the practical knowledge of textual preparation, privileges, dedications, typography, and commercial calculation that would later sustain his own publishing activity. A journey to Rome shortly before February 1550, undertaken in the hope that the accession of his godfather Julius III might secure him a curial position, proved unsuccessful, and he returned to Venice. He married Benedetta Musocca, or Misocca, the daughter of the Venetian merchant Vettore Musocca; their children included Iacopo, Fiorenza, and Aurora. In 1554 he definitively abandoned legal practice for the profession of letters.Sansovino’s mature career cannot be adequately described by the modern categories of author, translator, editor, publisher, and bookseller, since he repeatedly combined these functions within a single enterprise. His programme was rooted in the conviction, widely debated among the Infiammati, that the vernacular could make historical, philosophical, technical, and political knowledge available to a readership extending beyond the universities and the learned professions. His publications therefore encompassed medicine and anatomy, rhetoric and oratory, grammar, letter writing, law, history, political institutions, chivalric orders, genealogy, literature, and contemporary warfare. Among the characteristic products of this activity were L’edificio del corpo humano of 1550; his Italian rendering of Aristotle’s De anima in 1551; the juridical dialogue L’avocato, first printed in 1554; collections of vernacular orations; editions and commentaries devoted to Dante, Petrarch, Boccaccio, Ariosto, Bembo, and Sannazaro; and numerous translations or compilations derived from Latin, Italian, Spanish, and other sources. His editorial procedures ranged from translation and abbreviation to compilation, rearrangement, annotation, linguistic revision, and the construction of elaborate paratextual frameworks. Authorship in his books is consequently often collective or stratified rather than unitary, and modern scholarship has shown that the apparently heterogeneous catalogue was governed by recognisable editorial strategies and by close attention to the requirements of the Venetian market.In 1560 Sansovino began publishing and printing on his own account, initially in association with the physician Nicola Tinto. His enterprise employed devices centred upon the crescent moon, including a device accompanied by the motto In Dies, and was accordingly identified with the sign of the Moon. The first years were particularly productive, with imprints appearing under formulas naming Sansovino and his associates; at other times he acted as publisher while employing such printers as Francesco Rampazetto, Stefano Zazzera, the Bonelli, and Daniele Zanetti. He republished established vernacular authors when privileges or commercial circumstances made their texts available, while also issuing medical books, historical compilations, anthologies, and his own works. The undertaking was not uniformly prosperous, and the number of new titles fluctuated considerably, yet the surviving editions demonstrate an unusually sustained passage from service within other workshops to the direction of a recognisable editorial list. Sansovino was enrolled in the Venetian guild of printers and booksellers, although his attempt to obtain a place on its council in 1578 was unsuccessful. His professional identity was expressed with particular clarity in the tripartite classification he gave to his own production: compositions, translations, and collections.Political and historical writing formed one of the most persistent divisions of his work. Del governo dei regni et delle repubbliche, first published in 1561 and subsequently enlarged, assembled descriptions of ancient and modern constitutions in a comparative vernacular repertory. Its sources included Gasparo Contarini, Paolo Giovio, Francesco Guicciardini, Guillaume Postel, Alfonso de Ulloa, Ortensio Lando’s version of Thomas More, and writings by Machiavelli, some of which were incorporated without acknowledgement. Sansovino’s histories of the Ottoman dynasty and Turkish expansion responded to a substantial contemporary demand for information about the Ottoman world, particularly during the wars culminating in the battle of Lepanto. His Concetti politici of 1578 transformed passages from classical and modern historians and political writers into portable maxims intended for governors of republics and principalities. Although Machiavelli was omitted from the declared authorities, a substantial portion of the collection derived from the Discorsi, Il principe, Arte della guerra, and Istorie fiorentine. The collection was repeatedly reprinted and entered English circulation in Robert Hitchcock’s 1590 translation, Quintessence of Wit. Such works are less appropriately judged as claims to philosophical originality than as instruments for reorganising, moderating, and disseminating politically sensitive material among new classes of readers.The most influential of his practical manuals was Del secretario, first issued in four books in 1564 and expanded under his supervision to seven books in 1580. It joined instruction in epistolary composition to formulas of address, model letters, historical documents, and examples drawn from princely and administrative correspondence. In its enlarged form the work also became a carefully managed representation of Sansovino’s own career and patronage, since it incorporated letters sent to him by eminent correspondents and concluded with his autobiographical account to Gianfilippo Magnanini. Its repeated editions, continuing after his death into the seventeenth century, testify to its utility in a period of expanding diplomatic, secretarial, and bureaucratic practice. The manual exemplifies Sansovino’s characteristic ability to convert heterogeneous archival and literary materials into an accessible professional repertory.Sansovino’s enduring reputation rests above all upon Venetia città nobilissima et singolare, published in 1581 in fourteen books. This extensive description developed out of shorter guides to the city, including Tutte le cose notabili e belle che sono in Venetia, issued under the pseudonym Anselmo Guisconi in 1556, and the enlarged Delle cose notabili che sono in Venetia. The mature work integrated topography, ecclesiastical and secular architecture, works of art, magistracies, laws, ceremonies, social customs, princely biographies, writers, patrician families, and the history of the Republic. It drew not only upon printed histories but also upon private family records, monastic erudition, inscriptions, and privileged access to Venetian cultural networks. Although its factual reliability is uneven and its interpretation participates in the political mythology of Venice, it remains an indispensable witness to the city’s monuments, collections, institutions, and self-representation in the later sixteenth century. Its usefulness was recognised by Giovanni Stringa, who corrected and substantially enlarged it in 1604, and by Giustiniano Martinioni, who incorporated Stringa’s material and continued the account to 1663. After Jacopo Sansovino’s death in 1570, Francesco inherited his father’s estate and also contributed to the preservation and reshaping of the architect’s public memory. In 1573 he assumed the title of a knight of the Constantinian Order. Increasing visual impairment afflicted his final years, but he continued to revise, compile, and publish until shortly before his death. He dictated his testament on 24 November 1582 and died in Venice on 28 September 1583 after a fever lasting twelve days; he was buried in the church of San Geminiano. In April 1584 his son Iacopo transferred to Altobello Salicato the printing rights in his father’s privileged and unprivileged works, ensuring their continued circulation. Older criticism frequently treated Sansovino’s dependence upon earlier texts as evidence of haste or deficient originality. More recent scholarship has instead situated him within the material and collaborative conditions of the sixteenth-century book trade: as a mediator between learned culture and the vernacular market, an organiser of textual repertories, and one of the clearest representatives of the writer-publisher whose intellectual labour was inseparable from the production and commerce of printed books.
(Roma, 1521 – Venezia, 28 settembre 1583)

Contile Luca.name: Contile Luca
biographies: Luca Contile (1505–1574) occupies a distinctive, if secondary, place in the Italian literary landscape of the sixteenth century. Born in Cetona, near Siena, into a family of comfortable means but diminished noble status, Contile embodied the archetype of the Renaissance cortigiano—peripatetic, ambitious, intellectually versatile, yet perpetually constrained by the demands of patronage. His career unfolded across the courts of Rome, Milan, Naples, and the smaller principalities of northern Italy, mirroring the political and religious upheavals of the era: the splendor and moral ambiguities of Paul III’s Rome, the military campaigns of Charles V and Philip II, the tightening grip of Tridentine orthodoxy, and the gradual shift from the exuberant licentiousness of early Cinquecento humanism toward a more disciplined, often moralistic cultural climate.Origins and FormationContile was born in 1505 to a family whose fortunes had waned not through vice but through the father’s engagement in “mechanical” professions deemed beneath ancestral dignity. In his Ragionamento sopra la proprietà delle Imprese (1574), Contile provides valuable autobiographical details, noting that his paternal grandfather, also named Luca, had married into the Bevignati family of Perugia, which enjoyed ties to the powerful Baglioni. Despite these connections, the family’s social standing had slipped, a fact that appears to have fueled Contile’s lifelong attachment to his kin. Throughout his wanderings, he supported his mother and brothers Guidotto, Camillo, and Ceccante, and showed particular affection for his nephew Giovanni, whom he placed as secretary to Monsignor Michele Della Torre of Ceneda.His early education in Siena exposed him to the major vernacular authors and Latin, skills that enabled correspondence with friends like Federico Orlandini. He dabbled in philosophy, mathematics, and music, but these pursuits remained secondary to the vibrant social life of student brigades—swordplay, wrestling, ball games, and dances—which he later recalled nostalgically from Rome in 1541. The death of his father around 1520 coincided with renewed financial strain, yet Contile was sent to Bologna, where he attended the lectures of the Aristotelian Ludovico Boccadiferro. This period marked a shift from youthful enthusiasm to a more structured engagement with Aristotle’s Ethics and Rhetoric, influences traceable across his oeuvre, from the early Dialogi spirituali to the late Ragionamento. Philosophy, however, remained more an aspiration than a mastered discipline; the practical demands of court life soon prevailed.First Patronage: Agostino Trivulzio and Roman AcademiesIntroduced by Count Giulio Boiardo, Contile entered the service of Cardinal Agostino Trivulzio in Rome. The Eternal City under Paul III (Alessandro Farnese) dazzled the young provincial. In a letter, he painted a vivid, almost Pandoran portrait of a metropolis where virtue and vice coexisted: mercy for the poor, rewards for the learned, honors for soldiers, security from tyranny, and opportunities for merchants—yet also idleness, gambling, and courtesans. This judgment aligned with those of other aspiring literati drawn by Farnese patronage. Contile participated in academies such as the Virtù, Poesia nova, and Sdegno, environments characterized by verbal licentiousness that gradually yielded to Counter-Reformation restraint.His associations included figures like Annibal Caro, with whom he shared cultural preparation, friendships, and genres (epistolography and comedy). Contile mingled with “Berneschi” poets—Gandolfo Porrino, Francesco Bini, Girolamo Ruscelli—sharing their salacious adventures and “sciamannata” discourses, but also their intellectual isolation and parasitic dependence on patrons. Service to Trivulzio was neither onerous nor constant, yet Contile frequently complained of lost autonomy. Notable episodes include accompanying the cardinal to Lucca for Charles V’s entry (1541), where he offered a sharply observed, almost satirical portrait of the emperor’s worn attire, and a wintry halt at Montefiascone, described in letters echoing Caro’s travel miseries. Tensions arose over the delayed marriage of Trivulzio’s nephew Giovanni to Laura Gonzaga, for which Contile had stood guarantor. By 1542–44, he had shifted allegiance toward Alfonso d’Avalos, Marquis del Vasto.Dialogi spirituali and Ideological CommitmentThe Dialogi spirituali (Rome, 1543), elaborated in Milan in 1542 and encouraged by Boiardo and Vittoria Colonna, emerged from this Roman phase. Dedicated to religious conversations among acquaintances from Bologna and Trivulzio’s circle (Pallavicini, Boiardo, Landi, Trivulzio women), the five dialogues address core doctrines: the Trinity, the uniqueness of Christian faith, Jewish obstinacy regarding the Messiah, the afterlife, and the path to heaven. Lacking speculative depth, they articulate a rigid orthodoxy hostile to Reformation currents, vehement against Luther, critical of the Franco-Turkish alliance, and admiring of a strong Catholic defender—whether Charles V or, later, Philip II. Contile’s swift abandonment of lingering reformist sympathies (linked to Colonna) in favor of Tridentine authoritarianism is striking and consistent with his later political sentiments. Tolomei praised their doctrine and spirit while critiquing the grammar.Milan, Naples, and Theatrical ProductionConditions improved markedly at the court of Alfonso d’Avalos in Milan. Educated in chivalric ideals and surrounded by literary influences (Colonna, Costanza d’Avalos), the marquis and his wife Maria d’Aragona fostered a splendid environment. Contile engaged with Pietro Aretino, Paolo Giovio, Girolamo Muzio, and Giulio Camillo. He followed d’Avalos to Germany for the Diet of Worms (1545), expressing curiosity about Luther while handling lesser literary disputes. After d’Avalos’s death in 1546, Contile accompanied Maria d’Aragona to Pavia (where he joined Alciato’s “Chiave d’oro” academy) and Naples/Ischia, before a rupture in 1548 forced his departure.The second Milanese period under Ferrante Gonzaga proved most fruitful literarily. Contile produced La Trinottia (first printed 1542, revised 1550), a Sienese comedy of vices—avarice (Filargiro), lust (Brondio), pride (Icanio)—resolved through intrigue but punished intrinsically by the vices themselves. The prologue personifies human life in its variety. This moral integralism distinguishes Contile’s theater. La Pescara (1550) explores virtuous friendship between Lucio and Curzio amid romantic complications, resolved by anagnorisis; styled a “commedia grave,” it blends pathetic moralism with urban realism, drawing heavily on Plautus. La Cesarea Gonzaga (performed 1549, printed 1550) for a Gonzaga festivity honoring Philip of Austria features cross-dressing and simplified intrigue subordinated to moral acceptability.Subsequent pastorals—Nice (1551) and Argia (1552)—shift toward mythological and encomiastic modes suited to courtly demands, intertwining tragic myths (Adonis, Acis) or Diana’s chastening of sensual love with allegorical representations of Gonzaga figures. The Discorso sopra li cinque sensi del corpo (c. 1552), a commentary on a sonnet by Giuliano Goselini, reveals Contile’s erudition, legitimizing commentary traditions from Pico to Varchi and Savonarolan influences on sensory perception and ideal beauty.Later Wanderings and the RagionamentoService with Cardinal Cristoforo Madruzzo (1552–57) involved travel to the Diet of Augsburg and Milan, alongside pro-Spanish writings like Le sei sorelle di Marte (1556). Subsequent moves—to Ottavio Farnese, Sforza Pallavicino in Venice (where he knew Ruscelli, Dolce, Tasso, Patrizi), and back to Milan and Pavia—reflect chronic economic pressures and restless ambition. In Pavia, as commissioner of the estimo, he enjoyed relative serenity and produced his culminating work, the Ragionamento sopra la proprietà delle Imprese (1574), dedicated to the Accademia degli Affidati. Here Contile distinguishes imprese from related forms (devices, emblems, hieroglyphs), defines the impresa as “componimento di figura e di motto” representing a virtuous design, restricts their use to the magnanimous, and provides biographical notices on academicians, including himself. Though theoretically ambitious, its greatest value lies in these personal and historical details.His Rime (1560, with additions) and Lettere (1564) complete the corpus. The former, including fifty sonnets on Giovanna d’Aragona praised by Francesco Patrizi, remain occasional and encomiastic. The letters lack Aretino’s force or Caro’s brio but offer poignant autobiographical insights into the miseries of courtly servitude: loss of self, friends, family, and ultimately spiritual well-being. Contile died in Pavia on 28 October 1574, active among the Affidati under the academic name “Guidato,” with friends like Giambattista Pico as executor.Additional translations (Istitutioni dell’Imperio, 1558; Origine degli elettori, 1559) and lost works (Virgil translation, duel discourse, academy lectures) attest to ongoing scholarly activity.LegacyLuca Contile exemplifies the challenges facing mid-sixteenth-century Italian intellectuals: the tension between humanistic versatility and courtly dependence, between moral aspiration and practical compromise, and between lingering Renaissance vitality and Counter-Reformation discipline. His theater evolves from balanced moral comedy toward edifying gravity and pastoral encomium, reflecting broader cultural shifts. While lacking the genius of major contemporaries, Contile’s works illuminate the texture of court life, the networks of patronage, and the ideological currents of Tridentine Italy. His Ragionamento and letters remain valuable sources for the history of academies, imprese, and the lived experience of the Renaissance man of letters caught between ambition and necessity. In an age of grand syntheses, Contile offers the instructive portrait of a capable, reflective, and ultimately representative figure.His life and writings repay study not for transcendent originality but for the clarity with which they document the social, literary, and spiritual negotiations of a turbulent century.
(Cetona, 1505 – Pavia, 28 ottobre 1574)

Severino Marco Aurelio.name: Severino Marco Aurelio
biographies: Marco Aurelio Severino (Tarsia, Calabria, 2 November 1580–Naples, 15 July 1656) was a physician, surgeon, anatomist, natural philosopher, and man of letters whose career joined hospital practice and university teaching to the learned culture of seventeenth-century Naples and the wider European republic of letters. He was born to the jurist Giovan Giacomo Severino and Beatrice Oranges. After his father’s early death, his education was directed by his mother and his uncle Antonio. He studied locally at Tarsia and Roggiano, acquired the classical languages at Cosenza under the Jesuit Orazio Giannino, and was initially intended for the law. On moving to Naples, however, he attended the Jesuit college and then turned decisively to medicine at the Neapolitan Studio. His intellectual formation extended well beyond the statutory medical curriculum. He frequented the private school of the mathematician and natural philosopher Nicola Antonio Stigliola and came into contact with Tommaso Campanella during the latter’s imprisonment in Castel Nuovo. Campanella’s defence of philosophical liberty, together with the naturalism of Bernardino Telesio and the experimental interests associated with Giambattista Della Porta and the Lincean milieu, contributed to Severino’s enduring hostility to an exclusively scholastic Aristotelianism.On 1 February 1606 Severino received the doctorate of philosophy and medicine from the medical college of Salerno. After a brief return to Calabria, he settled permanently in Naples in 1608 and entered the circle of Giulio Jasolino, the Calabrian physician and anatomist whose practice united medicine, surgery, and natural inquiry. Late that year Severino assisted Jasolino at the post-mortem examination of the Theatine Andrea Avellino. He subsequently established himself in private practice and within the extensive hospital system attached to the city’s charitable institutions. By 1612 he belonged to the Accademia degli Oziosi, one of the principal centres of Neapolitan literary and scientific sociability. There he encountered scholars and physicians connected, directly or indirectly, with Federico Cesi’s Accademia dei Lincei, including Mario Schipano and Fabio Colonna. Severino treated Colonna in 1629, but their association was of earlier date; Colonna’s recommendation helped to make Severino known to Johann Faber in Rome. In 1625 Severino was proposed, without success, for admission to the Lincei as a royal physician and anatomist of Naples.In 1622 Severino won appointment as reader in surgery at the Neapolitan Studio. Anatomy was central both to his teaching and to the reputation he acquired through private and hospital practice. His surviving writings record a substantial clinical and pathological casuistry, including the post-mortem examination of Marcello Sacchetti, the Barberini associate and papal treasurer who died at Naples in 1629. Severino’s professional position nevertheless remained complicated by the traditional hierarchy separating learned physic from manual surgery. Modern scholarship has accordingly interpreted his long delay in publishing, and his probable concealment behind the name of his assistant Tiberio Malfi in Il barbiere (1626; recast in 1629 as Nuova prattica della decoratoria manuale et della sagnia), as evidence of the uncertain intellectual status of surgical practice. His mature conception of the surgeon, by contrast, refused the subordination of operative skill to purely textual medicine: surgery was for him a rational and learned discipline grounded in anatomy, observation, accumulated cases, and direct intervention upon the body.Severino first published under his own name in 1632, after a successful operation upon a daughter of Fernando Afán de Ribera, duke of Alcalá and viceroy of Naples. The resulting De recondita abscessuum natura, printed at Naples by Ottavio Beltrano, was a wide-ranging investigation of abscesses, tumours, inflammations, deformities, and other pathological formations, supported by clinical histories and illustrations. It consciously continued the southern Italian tradition represented by Giovanni Filippo Ingrassia, teacher of Jasolino, while giving unusual prominence to visible lesions and operative treatment. An enlarged edition appeared at Frankfurt in 1643. Severino’s advocacy of energetic treatment by iron and cautery brought him into conflict with more conservative practitioners and contributed to his removal from the Hospital of the Incurables in 1635. His reputation abroad was nevertheless firmly established. William Harvey visited him at Naples in 1636, initiating a sustained correspondence in which George Ent also participated. Severino was among the Italian physicians who accepted the circulation of the blood comparatively early, although he sought to connect Harveyan circulation with unresolved questions concerning respiration, the formation of vital spirits, and the relation between air and water.A graver crisis arose in 1640, when former assistants and professional enemies denounced Severino to the diocesan Inquisition. The accusations combined allegations of irreligious conduct with matters of personal life, including the existence of his son Giacinto outside marriage. Severino underwent imprisonment and judicial examination and briefly fled Naples; by the autumn of 1641, however, he had recovered his position and resumed his intellectual and professional activity. At this moment his house became an important destination for northern European medical travellers. Johann Georg Volckamer, a physician from Nuremberg trained at Altdorf and Padua, lived with him in 1641–42 as assistant and secretary. On returning to Germany, Volckamer carried manuscripts and thereafter acted as Severino’s principal editorial intermediary, securing presses, patrons, and readers north of the Alps. Thomas Bartholin and Johann van Horne likewise visited Severino in 1644 during their academic travels. His correspondence extended to Cassiano dal Pozzo, Johann Vesling, John Houghton, Ole Worm, Pietro Castelli, and other physicians and naturalists; among the younger Neapolitans associated with his researches, Tommaso Cornelio was especially important.The principal monument of Severino’s anatomical work was the Zootomia democritaea, issued from the Endter press at Nuremberg in 1645 under Volckamer’s supervision. Based upon decades of dissections and observations of human beings and numerous animal species, it is among the earliest substantial early modern attempts to organize anatomy comparatively. Its title invoked Democritus as the exemplary investigator of animal bodies and as an alternative to Peripatetic authority. Severino treated anatomical comparison not merely as the description of differences but as a means of discerning analogies of structure and function throughout living nature. Human anatomy was consequently to be understood within a larger investigation encompassing quadrupeds, birds, fishes, invertebrates, and even minute organisms. Although his natural philosophy retained teleological, metaphysical, and microcosmic elements, he repeatedly insisted that inherited propositions should be tested against dissection and sensible evidence. The work thus occupies an intermediate position between Renaissance philosophical naturalism, humanist erudition, and the comparative anatomy developed later in the century.After relinquishing his university chair in 1645, Severino continued to publish actively. The De efficaci medicina appeared at Frankfurt in 1646 as an extensive defence and exposition of active surgical therapy; Vipera Pythia, devoted to the viper, venom, and medicinal experiment, followed at Padua in 1650. The Trimembris chirurgia was printed at Frankfurt in 1653, while the Therapeuta Neapolitanus, published at Naples in the same year, included an important catalogue of his printed and projected writings. The Seilo-phlebotome castigata appeared at Hanover in 1654. Other investigations remained unfinished or were published posthumously, notably the Antiperipatias of 1659, which assembled his arguments concerning the respiration of fishes and related zoological questions. The marked geographical dispersion of these editions—Naples, Frankfurt, Nuremberg, Padua, and Hanover—reflects both his European standing and his dependence upon correspondents and former pupils for the material transmission of his texts.Severino’s activities were not confined to medicine. As an Ozioso, under the academic name l’Assettato, he participated in the literary culture of Naples; his Querela della & accorciata appeared in 1644, and his commentary upon the poems of Giovanni Della Casa was printed posthumously by Antonio Bulifon in 1694. His intellectual remains were more extensive than his printed corpus. Roughly seventy volumes of manuscripts associated with him are now preserved in the Biblioteca Lancisiana in Rome, including correspondence, drafts, medical collections, and anatomical drawings. They passed through several hands before their acquisition for Giovanni Maria Lancisi’s library and remain indispensable for reconstructing Severino’s working methods, reading, clinical networks, and editorial projects. During the plague epidemic of 1656 he was summoned by the Neapolitan health authorities to participate in dissections intended to determine the nature of the contagion. He contracted the disease and died on 15 July, receiving an unmarked burial in the church of San Biagio Maggiore in the booksellers’ quarter. His historical importance lies in the conjunction he effected between learned surgery, pathological anatomy, comparative dissection, natural philosophy, and transnational scholarly communication, rather than in any simple claim that he anticipated a single later discipline.
(Tarsia, 2 novembre 1580 – Napoli, 12 luglio 1656)

Corvus Andreas.name: Corvus Andreas
biographies: Andrea Corvo, also known in Latin as Andreas Corvus, is a fascinating yet elusive figure in the history of Renaissance occult sciences. Active in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, he stands among the earliest systematic writers on chiromancy (palmistry) in Europe. Despite the considerable influence of his work, biographical details remain frustratingly scarce, and for centuries even his very existence was debated by scholars. His treatise on the reading of hands not only helped establish chiromancy as a respectable intellectual discipline during the Renaissance but also sparked heated polemics among practitioners of the divinatory arts.Life and Historical ContextCorvo was probably born around the middle of the fifteenth century in Carpi, in the territory of Modena. For a long time, his place of origin was uncertain because several early editions of his Chiromantia describe him as “Mirandulensis.” It is now generally accepted that he settled in Mirandola around 1470, likely following the appointment of Antonio de’ Corvi (possibly his brother-in-law) as provost of the city. Beyond this, almost nothing is known of his education, professional activities outside chiromancy, or the date and place of his death.What is clear is that Corvo practiced the art of chiromancy for many years and achieved sufficient renown to dedicate his principal work to Giovanni Francesco Gonzaga, Marquis of Mantua. This dedication served both as a plea for protection against “the bites of slanderers” and as an attempt to lend legitimacy to a divinatory practice often viewed with suspicion by religious and academic authorities.The Chiromantia and Its ControversiesCorvo’s fame rests almost entirely on his Chiromantia, one of the earliest printed treatises devoted exclusively to the reading of hands. Its publication toward the end of the fifteenth century places him at the forefront of a growing European interest in physiognomy and chiromancy, disciplines that sought to interpret the divine signatures inscribed in the human body.The work provoked strong reactions. The Bolognese astrologer and chiromancer Bartolomeo della Rocca, known as Cocles (Cocles), launched a particularly harsh attack in his Anastasis (1504). He repeatedly mocked Corvo, punning on his name by calling him the “black crow” (nero Corvo) or “the blackest crow,” accusing him of plagiarism — dressing himself in peacock feathers while remaining fundamentally a crow. Cocles conceded that Corvo was skilled in the practice of chiromancy but dismissed his theoretical contributions as worthless.Despite these criticisms, Corvo’s text enjoyed remarkable success. Numerous editions appeared under his name, and some of Cocles’s own works were later confused with or attributed to Corvo, creating lasting bibliographical confusion. Other prominent chiromancers, such as Patrizio Tricasso, also criticized him, reflecting the intense rivalries common among practitioners of these arts. The Church placed Corvo’s book on the Index of Forbidden Books, alongside the works of Cocles, Tricasso, Johannes ab Indagine, and Pietro d’Abano. Yet the philosopher Tommaso Campanella later defended chiromancy in his Atheismus triumphatus, arguing that practitioners like Corvo merely observed God’s signs in nature and sinned only when they overstepped their proper bounds.Corvo also received notable praise. Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim listed him among the leading chiromancers of the age, while the polymath Jean Taisnier highlighted the excellence of his graphical demonstrations of hand-reading.The Printed Editions and Manuscript TraditionThe most important early edition is the extremely rare Excellentissimi et singularis viri in Chiromantia exercitatissimi magistri Andreae Corvi Mirandulensis opus rarissimum de eadem chiromantiae facultate, dedicated to Giovanni Francesco Gonzaga. Printed without typographical indications but dated to the very end of the fifteenth century, this incunable consists of 88 leaves in Gothic characters. It features two full-page woodcuts and 156 smaller illustrations — a remarkable visual apparatus for its time.Subsequent editions and translations testify to the work’s popularity:Picta chyromantia (Venice, 1513)Italian translation Opera Noua de Maestro Andrea Coruo da Carpi (Venice, 1519 and 1530)French translation by Jehan de Verdellay, L’art de chyromance (early 16th century, with later editions in 1611 and 1878)German translation Ein schönes Büchlin der Kunst Chiromantia (Strassburg, 1515)A particularly interesting sixteenth-century manuscript copy survives in the Biblioteca Estense in Modena (Campori collection). This codex contains both physiognomy and chiromancy sections, along with 164 detailed plates illustrating the lines, mounts, and interpretive signs of the hand. A prologue (possibly by Cocles) precedes Corvo’s text, and the author carefully distinguishes between the right and left hands while offering practical reading instructions.Scientific and Cultural SignificanceWhile modern scholarship naturally views Corvo’s chiromantic doctrines as pseudoscientific, his work holds genuine historical importance. It represents an early attempt to systematize and illustrate the reading of hands through empirical observation combined with classical and medieval sources. The rich iconographic apparatus — hands meticulously divided into zones, lines, and “mounts” — made the text accessible and influential beyond learned circles.In the broader context of Renaissance culture, Corvo’s Chiromantia belongs to that fascinating borderland where medicine, natural philosophy, astrology, and divination intersected. Like many of his contemporaries, he believed that the hand was a microcosm reflecting both character and destiny, a visible manifestation of divine order. Though his theoretical framework was criticized even in his own time, the practical and visual dimension of his work ensured its longevity and inspired later generations of chiromancers and physicians.Today, the surviving editions and manuscripts of Andrea Corvo are prized as rare treasures of early printed books and as important documents in the history of Western esotericism. They remind us of a period when the human hand was considered not merely an instrument of labor but a profound text written by nature itself — one that the skilled reader might hope to decipher.
(fl. late 14th - Early 15th)

Fregoso Antonio.name: Fregoso Antonio
biographies: Antonio Fregoso, known variably as Campofregoso, Fulgoso, and later adopting the appellation Fileremo, emerges as a significant yet complex figure within the tapestry of Italian humanism during the transition from the 15th to the 16th century. Born around 1460 in Carrara, he was a scion of the noble Genoese Fregoso family, albeit through an illegitimate line. His life and works provide a window into the intricate interplay of politics, literature, and philosophy during the Italian Renaissance, a period marked by profound cultural and intellectual ferment.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative Education.Antonio Fregoso's birth into the Fregoso family, a lineage steeped in Genoese nobility, was complicated by his illegitimacy. His mother, Giovanna, remains an elusive figure in historical records, while his father, Spinetta Fregoso, played a pivotal role in his early life. Spinetta's political alliances, particularly with Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan, positioned young Antonio within a sphere of influence that would shape his future. The irregular legitimization of Antonio by Emperor Frederick III underscores the era's intricate web of political and familial negotiations. Following Spinetta's death in 1467, Antonio came under the tutelage of Cicco Simonetta, a testamentary guardian appointed by his father, which facilitated his integration into Milanese society. The grant of Milanese citizenship by Galeazzo Maria Sforza in 1472 further cemented his status, although subsequent political upheavals, including Simonetta's execution, would challenge his position.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual Networks.Antonio Fregoso's literary output reflects the intellectual currents of his time, blending classical influences with contemporary philosophical discourse. His notable works, 'Riso di Democrito' and 'Pianto di Heraclito,' written in 1505 and 1507, respectively, employ a dantesque structure to explore themes of laughter and sorrow, drawing upon the philosophical dichotomy of Democritus and Heraclitus. These works, alongside the 'Dialogo de Fortuna,' reveal Fregoso's engagement with notions of human fortune and virtue, resonating with the ideas of Erasmus and echoing the allegorical style of Ludovico Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso.' Fregoso's intellectual milieu included figures such as Lancino Curti, Bartolomeo Simonetta, and Gaspare Visconti, with whom he shared literary exchanges that enriched the cultural landscape of Lombardy.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing Circulation.The publication and dissemination of Fregoso's works were facilitated by the vibrant printing culture of Renaissance Italy. The typographical landscape of Milan and Genoa, characterized by the proliferation of humanist texts and the influence of the Aldine Press, provided a fertile ground for Fregoso's ideas. His works were not only circulated within Italy but also translated into French and Spanish, as evidenced by the translations by Michele d'Amboise and Alonso Lobera, respectively. This international reach underscores the broader impact of his writings and their alignment with the humanist ideals that transcended national boundaries.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring Legacy.Antonio Fregoso's legacy is marked by both recognition and obscurity. His mention in Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso' attests to his contemporaneous relevance, while later literary historians, such as Crescimbeni, acknowledged his philosophical inclinations. The allegorical richness of his works, situated between medieval and Renaissance sensibilities, reflects the transitional nature of his era. Despite the political vicissitudes that marred his life, Fregoso's contributions to Italian literature and philosophy endure, offering insights into the complexities of human fortune and the pursuit of wisdom.
(Carrara 1460 ca - 1530 ca)

Antonio Fregoso, known variably as Campofregoso, Fulgoso, and later adopting the appellation Fileremo, emerges as a significant yet complex figure within the tapestry of Italian humanism during the transition from the 15th to the 16th century. Born around 1460 in Carrara, he was a scion of the noble Genoese Fregoso family, albeit through an illegitimate line. His life and works provide a window into the intricate interplay of politics, literature, and philosophy during the Italian Renaissance, a period marked by profound cultural and intellectual ferment.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative Education.Antonio Fregoso's birth into the Fregoso family, a lineage steeped in Genoese nobility, was complicated by his illegitimacy. His mother, Giovanna, remains an elusive figure in historical records, while his father, Spinetta Fregoso, played a pivotal role in his early life. Spinetta's political alliances, particularly with Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan, positioned young Antonio within a sphere of influence that would shape his future. The irregular legitimization of Antonio by Emperor Frederick III underscores the era's intricate web of political and familial negotiations. Following Spinetta's death in 1467, Antonio came under the tutelage of Cicco Simonetta, a testamentary guardian appointed by his father, which facilitated his integration into Milanese society. The grant of Milanese citizenship by Galeazzo Maria Sforza in 1472 further cemented his status, although subsequent political upheavals, including Simonetta's execution, would challenge his position.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual Networks.Antonio Fregoso's literary output reflects the intellectual currents of his time, blending classical influences with contemporary philosophical discourse. His notable works, 'Riso di Democrito' and 'Pianto di Heraclito,' written in 1505 and 1507, respectively, employ a dantesque structure to explore themes of laughter and sorrow, drawing upon the philosophical dichotomy of Democritus and Heraclitus. These works, alongside the 'Dialogo de Fortuna,' reveal Fregoso's engagement with notions of human fortune and virtue, resonating with the ideas of Erasmus and echoing the allegorical style of Ludovico Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso.' Fregoso's intellectual milieu included figures such as Lancino Curti, Bartolomeo Simonetta, and Gaspare Visconti, with whom he shared literary exchanges that enriched the cultural landscape of Lombardy.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing Circulation.The publication and dissemination of Fregoso's works were facilitated by the vibrant printing culture of Renaissance Italy. The typographical landscape of Milan and Genoa, characterized by the proliferation of humanist texts and the influence of the Aldine Press, provided a fertile ground for Fregoso's ideas. His works were not only circulated within Italy but also translated into French and Spanish, as evidenced by the translations by Michele d'Amboise and Alonso Lobera, respectively. This international reach underscores the broader impact of his writings and their alignment with the humanist ideals that transcended national boundaries.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring Legacy.Antonio Fregoso's legacy is marked by both recognition and obscurity. His mention in Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso' attests to his contemporaneous relevance, while later literary historians, such as Crescimbeni, acknowledged his philosophical inclinations. The allegorical richness of his works, situated between medieval and Renaissance sensibilities, reflects the transitional nature of his era. Despite the political vicissitudes that marred his life, Fregoso's contributions to Italian literature and philosophy endure, offering insights into the complexities of human fortune and the pursuit of wisdom.
(Carrara 1460 ca - 1530 ca)

Berni Francesco.name: Berni Francesco
biographies: Francesco Berni (Ferrara, 1610–13 October 1673), not to be confused with the celebrated sixteenth-century Tuscan poet of the same name, was a Ferrarese jurist, civic official, professor of eloquence, academician, dramatist, librettist, and author of occasional and historical works. His career belongs to the cultural world of papal Ferrara after the devolution of the duchy in 1598, when municipal institutions, aristocratic households, academies, religious confraternities, and visiting princely courts jointly sustained an active culture of ceremonial oratory and theatrical spectacle. Berni served as secretary to the civic magistracy and was employed as its orator before Pope Innocent X and two of his successors. He also taught eloquence at the University of Ferrara. His position combined legal and rhetorical training with the practical duties of public representation: addresses, commemorations, festival descriptions, academic discourses, and dramatic texts were complementary aspects of a single professional identity.Academies provided one of the principal structures of Berni’s intellectual and social activity. He belonged to the Accademia dei Confusi, before which he delivered L’omicidio amoroso di Radamisto, an academic discourse drawn from the twelfth book of Tacitus’s Annals and printed by the ducal and camerale printer Francesco Suzzi in 1640. He was also prince of the Accademia degli Intrepidi and a founder of the Accademia dei Fileni, in which he bore the name L’Aggirato. These affiliations were not merely titular. His surviving publications show sustained participation in collective exercises that united rhetoric, historical exemplarity, poetry, music, and ceremonial display. L’Accademia raunatasi nel Castello di Ferrara il dì 16 giugno 1645, addressed to Marchese Ercole Trotti, records one such occasion, while the two-volume Dell’Accademia, printed at Ferrara in 1657–1658 by the episcopal printers Alfonso and Giovanni Battista Maresti, assembled a broader body of academic material. The edition was embellished with an engraved frontispiece by Silvestro Maria Curletti, an indication of the visual and bibliographical care accorded to Berni’s learned persona.Berni’s earliest securely documented activity already places him within the culture of the courtly festival. In 1631 he described a foot tournament and its allegorical invention, together with the piscatory fable Alcina maga, represented in the Sala dei Giganti at Ferrara during Carnival. His subsequent writings repeatedly served occasions involving distinguished visitors, marriages, funerals, and civic or dynastic commemoration. Le pretensioni del Tebro e del Po (1642), for which the poetic composition was supplied by Ascanio Pio di Savoia and the description by Berni, commemorated the arrival in Ferrara of Prince Taddeo Barberini. L’esequie trionfali del marchese Guido Villa (1656) documented the elaborate obsequies celebrated in the Ferrarese church of San Francesco. Such publications belong to the bibliographical category of the festival book: they preserved otherwise transient performances by recording their allegorical programmes, scenic actions, ceremonial structures, and political meanings.His historical interests are most conspicuous in De gli eroi della Serenissima Casa d’Este ch’ebbero il dominio in Ferrara, printed by Francesco Suzzi in 1640 and dedicated to Francesco I d’Este, Duke of Modena. Conceived as a sequence of lives commemorating the former rulers of Ferrara, the project remained incomplete: of the twenty-four biographies apparently planned, only five were published, treating Almerico, Tedaldo I, Bonifacio III, Matilda, and Azzo VIII. The volume contained an engraved title and five portrait plates. Contemporary prefatory evidence associated its engravings with Catarino Doino, although the attribution and relationship between these plates and other contemporary series of Este portraits remain bibliographically problematic. Berni’s work participated in a competitive antiquarian and iconographic enterprise through which seventeenth-century authors and engravers reconstructed Este genealogy after the dynasty’s removal from Ferrara. Its combination of historical narrative and portraiture also exemplifies the close collaboration among author, engraver, and printer characteristic of local commemorative publishing.Berni’s most sustained contribution was to musical theatre. In Ferrara he worked within a relatively stable collaborative group comprising the composer Andrea Mattioli, the theatrical engineer Carlo Pasetti, and the patron and organizer Cornelio Bentivoglio. Mattioli set Berni’s La palma d’amore, performed at the theatre of San Lorenzo during Carnival 1650 for the marriage of Francesco Maria Estense Mosti and Caterina Pio di Savoia, and Il ratto di Cefalo, staged on 26 June 1650 in the theatre of the Sala Grande with machinery devised by Pasetti.Il ratto di Cefalo was revived during the following Carnival, when Berni’s L’esiglio d’Amore, composed by Mattioli in collaboration with Filiberto Laurenzi, was likewise performed; the latter was repeated in May 1651 with a new prologue honouring the papal legate Benedetto Odescalchi. The same Ferrarese circle produced Gli sforzi del desiderio, described as a dramatic-musical recreation and mounted in Palazzo Miroglio in 1652 for the passage of the archdukes of Tyrol, and L’Antiopa, performed in the Sala Grande on 23 and 24 February 1653. These works disclose a dramaturgy conceived in conjunction with music, transformations, stage machinery, and the architecture of temporary performance rather than as an autonomous literary text.Berni’s reputation extended beyond Ferrara. He was favourably received by members of the Austrian archducal house and by the ducal courts of Parma and Mantua; in 1658 the Duke of Mantua conferred upon him the title of count. His connection with the Farnese court culminated in the festivities for the marriage of Ranuccio II, Duke of Parma, and Margherita Violante of Savoy in 1660. For the Teatro Farnese he wrote La Filo, overo Giunone rappacificata con Ercole, a musical drama associated with Francesco Manelli, and I sei gigli, a tournament intended for performance on a subsequent evening. Other compositions connected with the same nuptial celebrations included La gara degli elementi and Le ali d’Amore. In these works spoken and sung drama, dance, tournament, allegory, and dynastic compliment formed parts of a coordinated ceremonial programme. The geographical movement of Berni’s texts between Ferrara and Parma demonstrates the mobility of librettists, musicians, engineers, and printed festival descriptions within the courts and aristocratic networks of northern Italy.In 1666 Berni consolidated his dramatic reputation through I drami del signor conte Francesco Berni, da varie impressioni qui raccolti e ristampati, issued at Ferrara by Giulio Bolzoni Giglio and Giuseppe Formentini and dedicated to Ranuccio II. The collection detached a substantial portion of his theatrical writing from the ephemeral circumstances of individual performances and presented it as a coherent authorial corpus. This act of collection is important in the history of the libretto: like several other seventeenth-century dramatists, Berni sought to preserve texts originally printed as occasional performance books by gathering them into an edition intended for continued literary circulation. He nevertheless remained an occasional writer to the end of his life; an ode celebrating the marriage of Hebe and Hercules in honour of Cardinal Sigismondo Chigi, legate of Ferrara, appeared in 1673.Berni died at Ferrara on 13 October 1673, aged sixty-three. His historical significance rests less upon any single work than upon the unusually complete intersection represented by his career: university eloquence, municipal service, academy culture, historical commemoration, dynastic patronage, festival publishing, and opera. His writings document the mechanisms by which seventeenth-century spectacle was conceived, financed, performed, described, and transmitted in print. They also illuminate the professional transformation of the librettist from an occasional supplier of verse into a recognizable author capable of collecting, revising, and presenting his dramatic works under his own name.

Bosse Abraham.name: Bosse Abraham
biographies: Introduction & Humanist/Historical Signification. Abraham Bosse, born in 1602 in Tours, France, stands as a pivotal figure in the realm of 17th-century engraving, a period marked by the flourishing of baroque art and the burgeoning influence of scientific inquiry on artistic practices. His works, numbering over 1500 engravings, are not merely artistic expressions but serve as invaluable historical documents that capture the zeitgeist of Louis XIII's France, offering insights into the social customs, fashion, and furniture of the time.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative Education. Bosse was born into a family likely engaged in crafts or trade, a common background for many artists of the period, which provided him an early exposure to the intricacies of design and craftsmanship. His formative years in Tours, a city known for its vibrant cultural life and as a hub of artistic production, would have nurtured his artistic inclinations. Bosse's education in perspective under the tutelage of Girard Desargues, a prominent mathematician and engineer, was instrumental in shaping his technical precision and innovative approach to engraving. Desargues was a key figure in the development of projective geometry, and his influence on Bosse is evident in the latter's meticulous attention to spatial composition and depth in his works.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual Networks. Bosse's oeuvre is characterized by a keen observational acuity and a delicate sensibility, which he applied to a wide array of subjects. His series such as 'Le Jardin de la Noblesse Française' (1629) and 'La Noblesse Française en Église' (1630) offer a vivid portrayal of the French aristocracy, while 'Le Mariage à la Ville' and 'Le Mariage à la Campagne' (1633) provide contrasting views of urban and rural nuptial customs. His depiction of everyday scenes, such as 'Les Cris de Paris', echoes the genre scenes popularized by Dutch artists, yet with a distinctly French elegance. Bosse's religious and allegorical works, including 'Les Vierges Sages et les Vierges Folles' and 'Les Quatre Saisons', reflect the period's fascination with moral and philosophical themes, rendered with a baroque theatricality. His intellectual network included associations with the Academy of Painting, where he initially taught before his expulsion in 1661 due to ideological clashes with Charles Le Brun, the Academy's autocratic director. This conflict highlights the tension between individual artistic expression and institutional control during this era.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing Circulation. The publication of Bosse's 'Traité des manières de graver en taille-douce' in 1645 marks a significant contribution to the technical literature on engraving, providing a comprehensive guide to the art of copperplate engraving, a method that would dominate printmaking for centuries. This treatise, reprinted multiple times, underscores the enduring relevance of his technical insights. The typographical context of 17th-century Paris, a city at the forefront of printing and book production, facilitated the wide circulation of Bosse's works, contributing to his reputation across Europe. Parisian printers and publishers, benefiting from the city's status as a cultural and intellectual capital, played a crucial role in disseminating his engravings, which were valued not only for their aesthetic qualities but also as educational tools and collectibles.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring Legacy. Bosse's work was met with critical acclaim during his lifetime, though his career was not without controversy, particularly his exclusion from the Academy of Painting, which reflects broader debates about artistic autonomy and institutional authority. Despite these challenges, his engravings have been celebrated for their technical mastery and nuanced portrayal of contemporary life. His influence extends beyond his immediate period, impacting subsequent generations of artists and engravers. The enduring legacy of Abraham Bosse is evident in the continued scholarly interest in his work, as evidenced by the numerous studies and catalogues dedicated to his oeuvre. His engravings remain a vital resource for historians and art historians alike, offering a window into the social fabric and artistic milieu of 17th-century France.

Cirino Andrea.name: Cirino Andrea
biographies: Andrea Cirino (Messina, 1618–Palermo, 6 September 1664) was a Theatine cleric, preacher, antiquarian, and compiler of works encompassing sacred exegesis, classical philology, natural history, and Roman antiquities. Early Theatine biographers describe him as belonging to a noble Messinese family. He entered the Congregation of the Clerics Regular while still an adolescent and made his solemn profession at Messina on 5 July 1634. His intellectual formation joined the scholastic and scriptural disciplines required by his order to an unusually extensive reading of pagan antiquity. Contemporary and near-contemporary accounts repeatedly emphasize his capacious memory, facility in retrieving passages from the Fathers and classical authors, and ability to employ this accumulated learning in preaching. Such testimony is conventionally encomiastic, but it corresponds closely to the conspicuously compilatory structure of his surviving publications.Cirino’s religious career was associated particularly with Messina and with the Theatine house of San Giuseppe in Palermo. He acquired a reputation as a preacher and was remembered for addressing the Palermitan populace during a period of civic disorder, urging the restoration of tranquillity. His earliest identified publication is the funeral oration delivered for Cardinal Giannettino Doria, archbishop of Palermo, printed there by Decio Cirillo in 1643. A devotional discourse for the Messinese feast of the Madonna della Lettera followed at Monteleone in 1649. These works place him firmly within the public culture of the seventeenth-century religious orator, in which sermons and ceremonial addresses served simultaneously as instruments of pastoral instruction, civic representation, and learned display.His most distinctive contribution, however, lay in the immense antiquarian compilations devoted to hunting and animals. The Variarum lectionum, sive De venatione heroum libri duo, printed at Messina by the heirs of Pietro Brea in 1650, examined the origins, practices, and cultural meanings of hunting through an accumulation of testimonia drawn from classical, Christian, historical, and mythographical literature. This enterprise was enlarged in the De venatione et natura animalium libri quinque, issued at Palermo by Giuseppe Bisagni in 1653. The publication is bibliographically complex, comprising separately titled sections, among them the extensive De natura et solertia canum and a book on fishes. Its title advertises the consultation of approximately thirty thousand passages from earlier authors, an assertion characteristic of Cirino’s conception of scholarship as the ordered recovery of an encyclopaedic textual inheritance. The work treats animals not solely as physical creatures but also as scriptural signs, medical substances, political and moral exempla, objects of legal or ritual practice, and witnesses to the customs and migrations of ancient peoples. Its woodcut illustrations and multipart organization also give it a notable place among the scientific and antiquarian books produced by the Palermitan press in the middle decades of the seventeenth century. Although sometimes classified as natural history, its governing method is more accurately described as sacred and classical erudition than as experimental zoology.Cirino’s interests extended beyond animal lore. His Historia delle cause et effetti della peste, published at Genoa in 1656, addressed the epidemic through the medical, historical, providential, and moral categories available to a learned cleric of his age. In 1657 he published at Naples a life of the Theatine Francesco Olimpio. He is also associated with the account of the festivities held in Naples for the birth of Philip Prospero, Prince of Asturias, an example of the richly illustrated festival literature generated within the dominions of the Spanish Habsburgs. His work thus moved between several characteristic forms of Baroque print culture: the occasional oration, devotional biography, civic and dynastic celebration, epidemic history, and large-scale Latin compilation. Modern scholarship has also drawn attention to his connection with the mathematician and natural philosopher Giovanni Alfonso Borelli, describing Cirino as a friend and supporter within the intellectual environment of seventeenth-century Messina and Rome.At his death Cirino left a substantial body of unpublished material. Theatine bibliographers record commentaries on the Apocalypse and other books of Scripture, together with writings on duties, Epictetus and constancy, Platonic philosophy, medicine, prodigies, and apparitions of the Cross. The present whereabouts or survival of all these manuscripts cannot be securely established. His principal posthumous publication was the Variarum lectionum de urbe Roma eiusque conditore Romulo liber singularis, printed at Palermo by Agostino Bossio in 1665 under the supervision of his confrère Francesco Maria Maggio. Devoted to Rome and its founder, it applied Cirino’s characteristic method of cumulative textual comparison to chronology, foundation legends, institutions, religion, and the antiquarian problems surrounding Romulus. The work subsequently entered wider European antiquarian circulation when Albert-Henri de Sallengre included it in the second volume of his Novus thesaurus antiquitatum Romanarum, published at The Hague in 1718.Cirino died in the Theatine house at Palermo after prolonged illness, attributed by early biographers to incessant preaching and study. The best early evidence places his death on 6 September 1664, although some later accounts give 7 September. His posthumous reputation rested less upon an original system of natural or historical explanation than upon the amplitude and organization of his learning. He belongs to the learned ecclesiastical culture of Spanish Sicily in which biblical interpretation, patristics, classical antiquities, civic history, medicine, and natural lore remained mutually permeable fields. His books are consequently important not only for their particular subjects—especially hunting, dogs, fishes, and Roman origins—but also as material witnesses to the compilation, illustration, and printing of encyclopaedic scholarship in seventeenth-century Messina and Palermo.

Graziani Girolamo.name: Graziani Girolamo
biographies: Girolamo Graziani (1 October 1604–11 September 1674) was an Italian poet, diplomat, and statesman whose career unfolded at the intersection of the literary culture and political life of the seventeenth-century Este court. Born in Pergola in the Duchy of Urbino, he spent much of his adult life in the service of the Este dynasty in Modena, combining administrative and diplomatic responsibilities with an extensive literary production that included epic poetry, panegyric verse, political and historical writings, and tragedy. His principal works, particularly Il conquisto di Granata (1650) and Il Cromuele (1671), place him among the significant representatives of seventeenth-century Italian literary culture.Graziani was born in Pergola on 1 October 1604 to Antonio Graziani and Lavinia. His father served first as a uditore di rota in Ferrara and subsequently held important judicial offices in Modena. In 1619 the family moved to Modena, where Graziani continued his education. He studied at Parma and Bologna and obtained degrees in both jurisprudence and the humanities. His early formation consequently combined literary studies with the legal and administrative culture that would later prove essential to his career at the Este court.Graziani began publishing at a remarkably young age. In 1621, when he was seventeen, he published his first collection of verse, Rime di Girolamo Graziani della Pergola, in Parma. The volume contained love poetry as well as panegyric compositions addressed to members of the Este and Della Rovere families.His political career developed gradually. After the death of Duke Cesare d'Este in 1628 and the abdication of Alfonso III, Graziani was appointed secretary to the ducal princes. In 1632 he entered the personal service of Prince Obizzo d'Este, brother of Duke Francesco I, and during the following years he began to undertake diplomatic missions on behalf of the Este state. His early career was interrupted in 1641 by a political conflict surrounding Obizzo's unsuccessful attempt to obtain the cardinalate, after which Graziani was forced to leave Modena and returned to Pergola.Graziani's early literary production included La Cleopatra, an epic poem first published at Modena in 1631 and subsequently expanded and reissued. The poem established his reputation among contemporary men of letters and already displayed his characteristic interest in combining historical subjects, emotional and pathetic episodes, and dynastic themes.His major achievement in epic poetry was Il conquisto di Granata, first published at Modena by Bartolomeo Soliani in 1650. The poem consists of twenty-six cantos in ottava rima and recounts the final phase of the Christian conquest of Granada in 1492. Its narrative combines warfare, love, disguise, supernatural intervention, religious themes, and historical material, while drawing upon the traditions of Italian chivalric and heroic poetry.Contrary to some later characterizations of the poem as a straightforward continuation of Marino's poetic style, its language and structure are more complex. The poem is relatively restrained in its use of concettismo and combines epic, romance, magical, historical, and pathetic elements. Its final cantos also contain significant political and religious allusions, including prophecies concerning Christian expansion and the appearance of Christopher Columbus, whose role connects the conquest of Granada with the subsequent expansion of Christianity beyond Europe. The first edition was dedicated not to Louis XIV or Cardinal Mazarin, but to Francesco I d'Este, Duke of Modena. The dedication was rewarded by the duke with an annual pension of 200 scudi, in addition to Graziani's existing salary.Graziani's return to Modena in 1647 marked the beginning of the most important phase of his political career. He succeeded Fulvio Testi as secretary to Alfonso d'Este, son of Francesco I, and in December 1648 was sent to Paris on a diplomatic mission to seek French assistance for Modena in its war against Spain. His mission coincided with the Fronde, and his negotiations were facilitated in part by his relationship with Cardinal Mazarin.In July 1652 Graziani was formally appointed Segretario di Stato. In this capacity he accompanied Cardinal Rinaldo d'Este to Rome and was present during the conclave of 1655 that elected Pope Alexander VII. In 1658, in recognition of his services, he received the fief of Sarzano in the Duchy of Reggio together with the title of count. Under Duke Alfonso IV, who succeeded Francesco I in 1658, Graziani retained an important position at court and was appointed Consigliere di Stato.His diplomatic activity continued during the regency of Laura Martinozzi. One of his most significant diplomatic achievements came in 1673, when he helped negotiate the marriage of Maria Beatrice d'Este, daughter of Alfonso IV and Laura Martinozzi, to James, Duke of York, the future James II of England.Graziani participated in the literary academies and intellectual networks characteristic of seventeenth-century Italy. His membership in the Accademia dei Gelati of Bologna is documented by contemporary sources, including Ottavio Zani's Memorie, imprese e ritratti dei sigg. Accademici Gelati (1672).His literary activity was also closely connected with the ceremonial and political culture of the Este court. Works such as La gara delle stagioni (1652), Il trionfo della virtù (1660), and the panegyrics devoted to Cardinal Mazarin and Louis XIV demonstrate how his literary production functioned within the culture of dynastic celebration and political representation.The collection Varie poesie e prose, published at Modena by Soliani in 1662, brought together a substantial portion of his literary production and is particularly significant for understanding the relationship between his poetry, prose writings, courtly activities, and political thought. The collection also contains early evidence concerning the composition of Il Cromuele.Graziani's most distinctive contribution to political drama was Il Cromuele, a five-act tragedy dealing with the English Civil War, the execution of Charles I, and the rise of Oliver Cromwell. The work was conceived during the 1660s and was first printed in Bologna by the Manolessi press in 1671; a parallel Modenese edition was issued by Viviano Soliani in the same year. The Bologna edition is particularly notable for its material presentation. It contains an engraved frontispiece and five engraved folding plates illustrating scenes from the tragedy. The surviving copies therefore demonstrate the close relationship between literary drama, visual representation, and the culture of the illustrated book in seventeenth-century Italy.The tragedy transforms the recent history of England into a drama of tyranny, regicide, and political legitimacy. Cromwell is represented as an isolated and increasingly tyrannical figure, while Charles I is presented as a noble and just sovereign whose execution acquires the symbolic character of a political and familial crime. The historical events are thus adapted to a courtly and monarchical political framework appropriate to a work dedicated to Louis XIV. Rather than treating Il Cromuele simply as a precursor of later Enlightenment historical drama, it is more accurate to regard it as a significant example of seventeenth-century Italian political tragedy and of the ways in which recent European history could be transformed into courtly dramatic discourse.The publishing history of Graziani's works reflects the close relationship between literary production and courtly patronage. Il conquisto di Granata was first printed at Modena by Bartolomeo Soliani in 1650, while Il Cromuele appeared in Bologna from the Manolessi press and in Modena from the ducal press of Viviano Soliani in 1671. Both works subsequently circulated in additional editions, demonstrating the continuing interest in Graziani's poetry and drama. The illustrated Bologna edition of Il Cromuele is particularly important in this regard. Its engraved frontispiece and theatrical plates demonstrate how the printed book could function not merely as a textual vehicle but also as a visual extension of courtly and dramatic culture.Reception and Historical LegacyGraziani enjoyed considerable recognition during his lifetime, although his later reputation proved less stable. His Conquisto di Granata was repeatedly reprinted during the seventeenth century and was regarded by later critics as one of the most accomplished Italian epic poems produced after Tasso. Modern scholarship has emphasized the poem's ability to combine epic, romance, historical, magical, and pathetic elements rather than reducing it to a simple imitation of either Tasso or Marino.His political and diplomatic career also distinguishes him from the figure of the court poet in a narrowly literary sense. Graziani occupied several important offices in the Este administration, undertook diplomatic missions to Paris and Rome, received a comital title and territorial fief, and played a significant role in the diplomatic negotiations surrounding the marriage of Maria Beatrice d'Este and James, Duke of York.Graziani died at Pergola on 11 September 1674, after leaving Modena earlier that year. His career therefore represents an unusually close conjunction of literary production, courtly patronage, diplomatic service, and political communication in seventeenth-century Italy. His works, particularly Il conquisto di Granata and Il Cromuele, provide valuable evidence for the interaction between literary culture and political thought in the European Baroque.
